label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Scarcity & Cost

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: The foundation of every economic decision.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Scarcity

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: What scarcity means

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Scarcity refers to the situation in which the resources available are not enough to satisfy all people's wants.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Scarcity concerns whether resources are sufficient relative to people's wants, not whether their physical amount is absolutely small. It is a comparison of quantity available versus size of want.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Examples

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Not scarce: fresh air in an outdoor area

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Scarce: fresh air in a fire scene

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Scarcity does not imply unlimited wants. Even limited wants create scarcity when available resources are much smaller.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Opportunity Cost

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: The definition

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the highest-valued option forgone.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Limited resources force a choice; some options are forgone; the value of the best option forgone is the opportunity cost.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: A three-step method that works in most questions

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: State the choice and the decision moment.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Identify the scarce resources required — include money, time, effort, owned assets, and receipts forgone.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Identify and state the value of the highest-valued option forgone.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Two values to distinguish

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Benefit of the choice: the value of the option chosen to the decision maker.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Opportunity cost of the choice: the value of the highest-valued option forgone.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Preference order runs from the option with the highest value to the option with the lowest value.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Full Cost

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Full cost is the opportunity cost

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Full cost is the value (usually expressed in $) of the best alternative uses of all resources (money, time, satisfaction, etc.) necessarily forgone in making a choice.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Explicit cost

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Money expenditure made as a result of the current choice — e.g. ticket payment.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Implicit cost

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: The value of the best alternative use of self-owned resources or receipts forgone — e.g. earnings, rent, resale value, or time.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Full cost = explicit cost + implicit cost

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Check four kinds of resources before you cost a choice

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Money, time, and effort

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Income or receipts forgone

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Use of an asset already owned (e.g. a ticket, device, premises, another resource already held)

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Three situations change opportunity cost

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: The value of the current highest-valued option forgone rises or falls.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: The chosen option requires a different amount or type of scarce resource.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: A different option (a new option or an originally lower-ranked option) becomes the highest-valued option forgone.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Always identify what changed: the chosen option's benefit, the resources required, the identity of the best option forgone, or its value.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Three Opportunity-Cost Traps

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: 1. Benefit trap

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: A rise in the value of the chosen option does not by itself change its opportunity cost.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: 2. Ranking trap

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: A changed preference order or a new option matters only if it changes the highest-valued option forgone.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: 3. Past-payment trap

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Only options available at the decision moment can be forgone. A past cost that cannot now be recovered is excluded.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Remember

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Higher opportunity cost need not reduce popularity.

label: Scarcity & Cost
text: Higher money cost need not mean higher full cost.

label: Interest
text: Interest & Time Preference

label: Interest
text: Why a dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow.

label: Interest
text: Basics

label: Interest
text: Two perspectives on interest

label: Interest
text: To borrowers, interest is the cost of earlier availability of resources.

label: Interest
text: To lenders, interest is the compensation for deferred availability of resources.

label: Interest
text: Borrowers choose to obtain something earlier. Lenders choose to obtain something later instead of now.

label: Interest
text: Positive time preference

label: Interest
text: People generally prefer the same amount of the same good earlier rather than later, because the value of current consumption > the value of future consumption (of the same amount).

label: Interest
text: Example — Peter and Susan

label: Interest
text: Peter lent a comic book to Susan and received a Karina photocard. His book will be back in one week.

label: Interest
text: To Susan, the Karina photocard is the cost of earlier availability of the comic book.

label: Interest
text: To Peter, the Karina photocard is the compensation for deferred availability of the comic book.

label: Interest
text: Why Interest Exists

label: Interest
text: The core reason

label: Interest
text: Earlier consumption is itself an economic good, so people may pay for earlier access to resources.

label: Interest
text: Which situations may interest exist in?

label: Interest
text: Barter economy (an economy where money doesn't exist)

label: Interest
text: Economy without inflation

label: Interest
text: Economy without scarcity

label: Interest
text: Answer: (1) and (2). Interest can exist without money and without inflation. But it cannot exist without scarcity — in a world with no scarcity, you could obtain or produce anything without opportunity cost, so there would be nothing to pay for earlier access.

label: Interest
text: Interest Matters Even Without Borrowing

label: Interest
text: Two options

label: Interest
text: Option 1: buy it now.

label: Interest
text: Option 2: buy it later.

label: Interest
text: The price is not the interest. The value of choosing Option 2 is delaying the use of money. The benefit of choosing Option 2 is earning investment income during the time gained.

label: Interest
text: Worked Example

label: Interest
text: Lending a comic book

label: Interest
text: Decision: Peter chooses to lend his comic book to Susan for one week.

label: Interest
text: Resources forgone: the use of the comic book for one week.

label: Interest
text: Compensation received: a Karina photocard.

label: Interest
text: Cost to Susan: the photocard — she pays it to obtain the comic book one week earlier.

label: Interest
text: Benefit to Peter: the photocard, which compensates him for deferring his use of the book.

label: Allocation
text: Allocation & Economic Systems

label: Allocation
text: Who gets what, and how the rules decide.

label: Allocation
text: Competition and Allocation

label: Allocation
text: Why allocation is needed

label: Allocation
text: Scarcity forces a rule for deciding who gets what. The chain is:

label: Allocation
text: Scarcity

label: Allocation
text: Competing claims (competition)

label: Allocation
text: Allocation criterion Whose income is lower? Waiting time Rental

label: Allocation
text: Whose income is lower?

label: Allocation
text: Waiting time

label: Allocation
text: Rental

label: Allocation
text: Discrimination (who is selected)

label: Allocation
text: Price competition

label: Allocation
text: A type of competition based on users' willingness or ability to pay. The price need not be money. Exchanging a collectible toy for a ticket also reflects willingness and ability to pay.

label: Allocation
text: Non-price competition

label: Allocation
text: A type of competition based on criterion other than willingness or ability to pay, such as age, identity, queueing time, academic results, or a dress code.

label: Allocation
text: Tradition and custom

label: Allocation
text: Government decision

label: Allocation
text: Market exchange

label: Allocation
text: Ask what criterion decides allocation. Money is not required for price competition, and paying money does not automatically make every selection rule price competition.

label: Allocation
text: Goods vs Bads

label: Allocation
text: Classifying

label: Allocation
text: Is it a good or a bad? A good: some is preferred to none. A bad: less is preferred to more.

label: Allocation
text: A good: some is preferred to none.

label: Allocation
text: A bad: less is preferred to more.

label: Allocation
text: If it is a good, is it scarce? Economic good: quantity is insufficient for all wants. Free good: quantity is sufficient for all wants.

label: Allocation
text: Economic good: quantity is insufficient for all wants.

label: Allocation
text: Free good: quantity is sufficient for all wants.

label: Allocation
text: Supporting features

label: Allocation
text: Cost involved in production? — Yes for economic goods, No for free goods.

label: Allocation
text: More of them preferred? — Yes for economic goods, No for free goods.

label: Allocation
text: Willing to pay a price for more? — Yes for economic goods, No for free goods.

label: Allocation
text: Competition involved? — Yes for economic goods, No for free goods.

label: Allocation
text: Free-of-charge ≠ free good. The definition turns on whether available quantity is sufficient to satisfy all wants, not whether the official money price is zero.

label: Allocation
text: Willingness to pay identifies economic goods.

label: Allocation
text: Economic Systems

label: Allocation
text: The three basic economic questions

label: Allocation
text: Scarcity forces every society to answer these three questions:

label: Allocation
text: What to produce?

label: Allocation
text: How to produce?

label: Allocation
text: For whom to produce?

label: Allocation
text: Why the questions arise: limited resources cannot satisfy every want, so society must choose how resources and outputs are allocated.

label: Allocation
text: What to produce

label: Allocation
text: The choice of the types and quantities of goods and services to be produced.

label: Allocation
text: How to produce

label: Allocation
text: The choice of a production method or combination of scarce factor inputs: labour, entrepreneurship, capital and land.

label: Allocation
text: e.g. whether to replace human worker with AI/robots

label: Allocation
text: Use more labour: additional service workers

label: Allocation
text: Use more capital: AI chatbot services

label: Allocation
text: Changing the way a good is sold is not automatically a change in the production method. Identify the factor-input decision.

label: Allocation
text: For whom to produce

label: Allocation
text: The distribution of existing outputs — goods and services — among different users.

label: Allocation
text: Output is insufficient for every want

label: Allocation
text: Choose an allocation criterion Who can pay market price Who queue up first

label: Allocation
text: Who can pay market price

label: Allocation
text: Who queue up first

label: Allocation
text: Determine who can obtain the output

label: Allocation
text: If a case changes which users receive a good or service, it concerns for whom to produce.

label: Allocation
text: Economic system

label: Allocation
text: An economic system is distinguished by both the ownership of most resources and the main method by which those resources are allocated.

label: Allocation
text: Who owns most resources? Are they mainly owned by the government or by private individuals and firms? Does tradition decide who owns them?

label: Allocation
text: How are they mainly allocated? Do traditions, government decisions or market prices mainly decide how resources are used and who gets them?

label: Allocation
text: Traditional economy

label: Allocation
text: An economy that tackles the three basic economic problems mainly by customs and traditions.

label: Allocation
text: Customs and traditions determine the ownership and allocation of most resources. People follow rules and ways of doing things passed down over time.

label: Allocation
text: Example: In some New Territories villages, only males may share the property passed down by the family. Tradition decides who receives the property — this concerns for whom to produce.

label: Allocation
text: Planned or command economy

label: Allocation
text: An economy that tackles the three basic economic problems mainly by government decisions.

label: Allocation
text: Most resources are owned by the government and allocated by government decisions. The visible hand means the government directly decides how resources are allocated.

label: Allocation
text: Example: In Hong Kong, an income limit helps decide who may apply for public housing. This non-price criterion uses household income, not the rent people offer to pay. The income rule concerns for whom to produce. This one government service does not make the whole economy a planned economy.

label: Allocation
text: Market economy

label: Allocation
text: An economy that tackles the three basic economic problems mainly by the market mechanism.

label: Allocation
text: The market mechanism is a system under which resource allocation is guided by market prices. Most resources are allocated under price competition. The price mechanism is another name for the market mechanism.

label: Allocation
text: Prices help buyers and producers make choices: buyers compare prices when deciding what they are willing and able to buy; producers compare the prices of factor inputs when deciding which resources to use.

label: Allocation
text: The invisible hand: prices help guide these separate choices. No single authority has to decide every use of every resource.

label: Allocation
text: Most resources are owned by private individuals (households and firms), and their allocation is mainly guided by market prices.

label: Allocation
text: For whom to produce: a person who is willing and able to pay the fee can get tuition services from a private tutoring centre. The price helps decide who receives the service.

label: Allocation
text: How to produce: a firm compares the prices of AI chatbot services and labour when choosing its combination of factor inputs. The prices help it choose which resources to use.

label: Allocation
text: Private Property Rights

label: Allocation
text: Three exclusive rights

label: Allocation
text: Exclusive right to use — only the owner can decide how to use the property; no one else can use it without the owner's permission.

label: Allocation
text: Exclusive right to receive income — only the owner has the right to receive income generated from the property. Rent is payment for using property such as a house; licensing income is payment for permission to use property, such as a photograph. Ask who has the right to receive that income.

label: Allocation
text: Right to transfer — passing the property rights to another person, for example by selling or giving away the good.

label: Allocation
text: Clear delineation means it is clear who has each right and what that right allows. A prerequisite is something that must be in place first.

label: Allocation
text: Why clear rights matter

label: Allocation
text: Private property rights are clear.

label: Allocation
text: The price mechanism can be used.

label: Allocation
text: Resources can go to highest-valued users.

label: Allocation
text: Highest-valued users are those willing to pay the most for the resource. Clear rights let buyers and sellers know which rights are being exchanged.

label: Circular Flow
text: Circular Flow & Specialization

label: Circular Flow
text: How firms, households and markets fit together.

label: Circular Flow
text: The Circular Flow

label: Circular Flow
text: Four flows, two markets

label: Circular Flow
text: Four flows form one circular system: two economic units, two real flows, and two money flows in opposite directions.

label: Circular Flow
text: Firms

label: Circular Flow
text: Produce goods

label: Circular Flow
text: Demand factor services

label: Circular Flow
text: Receive sales revenue

label: Circular Flow
text: Pay production costs

label: Circular Flow
text: Households

label: Circular Flow
text: Consume goods and services

label: Circular Flow
text: Supply factor services

label: Circular Flow
text: Receive factor income

label: Circular Flow
text: Make consumption expenditure

label: Circular Flow
text: Three activities keep the economy moving

label: Circular Flow
text: Production: turning factors of production into goods and services.

label: Circular Flow
text: Consumption: using goods and services to satisfy human wants.

label: Circular Flow
text: Exchange: the buying and selling of goods and services.

label: Circular Flow
text: Do not collapse these activities into one idea: production creates output, consumption uses it, and exchange transfers it between parties.

label: Circular Flow
text: Two markets connect the units

label: Circular Flow
text: Product market: final goods and services are traded. In this model, the real flow from firms to households consists of final consumer goods and services. Firm output (goods & services): food, medicine, financial services.

label: Circular Flow
text: Factor market: factor services supplied by the owners of factors of production are traded. Factors include capital, land, labour and entrepreneurship. Factor services include labour and office premises.

label: Circular Flow
text: Factor services are real flows; factor income is the corresponding money flow.

label: Circular Flow
text: The same flow can have one name from the household perspective and another from the firm perspective.

label: Circular Flow
text: DSE exam lens

label: Circular Flow
text: Use this structure when sketching the model: draw and label the two economic units, the two real flows and the two money flows in opposite directions.

label: Circular Flow
text: Real Flow vs Money Flow

label: Circular Flow
text: Definitions

label: Circular Flow
text: Real flow: the flow of goods and services, including factor services.

label: Circular Flow
text: Money flow: the flow of monetary income and monetary expenditure.

label: Circular Flow
text: A real flow and its payment are two sides of the same transaction.

label: Circular Flow
text: Direction table

label: Circular Flow
text: Households → firms, money → Consumption expenditure (household view) / Sales revenue (firm view).

label: Circular Flow
text: Firms → households, real → Final consumer goods and services received / Final consumer goods and services supplied.

label: Circular Flow
text: Households → firms, real → Factor services supplied / Factor services received.

label: Circular Flow
text: Firms → households, money → Factor income / Production cost.

label: Circular Flow
text: Market value identity

label: Circular Flow
text: Market value in production = income generated in production = expenditure on final output.

label: Circular Flow
text: Same period, same final output: the value created by production generates income and is matched by expenditure on that final output.

label: Circular Flow
text: Intermediate goods are excluded when the market value of final output is measured.

label: Circular Flow
text: Specialization and Exchange

label: Circular Flow
text: Specialization

label: Circular Flow
text: Specialization: different people specialize in producing different goods and services.

label: Circular Flow
text: Specialize according to lower opportunity cost

label: Circular Flow
text: Opportunity cost identifies who should produce what.

label: Circular Flow
text: Two different comparisons

label: Circular Flow
text: Absolute comparison: who can produce more output with the same time or resources?

label: Circular Flow
text: Opportunity-cost comparison: who sacrifices less of the other good to produce one more unit?

label: Circular Flow
text: Absolute productivity is not the decision rule.

label: Circular Flow
text: Producing a good at a lower opportunity cost than another person means having a comparative advantage in that good.

label: Circular Flow
text: Exchange makes specialization feasible

label: Circular Flow
text: No opportunity for exchange.

label: Circular Flow
text: Each must be self-sufficient.

label: Circular Flow
text: Specialization cannot take place.

label: Circular Flow
text: Necessary does not mean sufficient: an opportunity for exchange permits specialization but does not by itself guarantee that people will choose to specialize.

label: Circular Flow
text: Difference between specialization and exchange

label: Circular Flow
text: Specialization changes the allocation of production. When production follows lower opportunity cost, it can increase total input.

label: Circular Flow
text: Exchange allows each specialist to obtain the good she no longer produces. It makes specialization feasible; it does not itself produce the extra output.

label: Circular Flow
text: Lower opportunity cost guides specialization; specialization changes production; exchange enables access to other goods.

label: Circular Flow
text: Positive vs Normative

label: Circular Flow
text: Positive statement

label: Circular Flow
text: A claim about the objective world that is refutable by facts.

label: Circular Flow
text: Claim about the objective world + evidence could show it is wrong = positive statement. A positive statement may be true or false.

label: Circular Flow
text: Normative statement

label: Circular Flow
text: A claim involving value judgement (subjective).

label: Circular Flow
text: Desirability: minimum wage legislation is undesirable.

label: Circular Flow
text: Priority: building artificial islands is more important for Hong Kong than reducing income inequality.

label: Circular Flow
text: Three cases — every claim belongs to one

label: Circular Flow
text: Positive

label: Circular Flow
text: Normative

label: Circular Flow
text: Neither: true by definition or logic and involves no value judgement.

label: Circular Flow
text: Example of "neither": "Triangles have three angles" is true by definition. It is not a claim that evidence could refute, and it contains no value judgement.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Demand, Supply & Equilibrium

label: Demand & Supply
text: Plans at all prices, and where they meet.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Demand

label: Demand & Supply
text: Definition

label: Demand & Supply
text: Demand is the set of quantities of a good that consumers are willing and able to buy at all corresponding prices over a period of time, other things being constant.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Would pay for the good.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Can afford the good.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Consider each possible price.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Same period; other things stay the same.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Demand is the whole buying plan across all these prices. At one price, the amount buyers are willing and able to buy is quantity demanded.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Want vs demand

label: Demand & Supply
text: Want: a desire to obtain a good, considered without regard to the cost of obtaining it.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Demand: the whole plan of quantities a consumer is willing and able to buy at all corresponding prices over a period.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Example: Mr Wan may want a $5.8 million Lamborghini Huracan STO, but if he cannot afford it, his quantity demanded is zero at the price of $5.8 million.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Demand curve, schedule and law

label: Demand & Supply
text: Demand curve: a graph showing the quantity demanded at each price.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Demand schedule: a table showing the quantity demanded at each price.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Law of demand: an increase in the price of a good will result in a decrease in its quantity demanded, and vice versa, other things being constant.

label: Demand & Supply
text: The law concerns the good's own price and a movement along the same demand curve.

label: Demand & Supply
text: A change in the good's own price moves along a given demand curve. When another factor affecting demand changes, the demand curve shifts.

label: Demand & Supply
text: The law of demand assures other things being constant. First ask whether another factor affecting demand changed.

label: Demand & Supply
text: No: other things stayed the same. Use the law of demand to explain how the good's own price affects quantity demanded.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Yes: another factor also changed. The change in quantity cannot be explained by the price change alone.

label: Demand & Supply
text: If price and quantity both rise, this alone does not show a violation of the law of demand.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Market Demand

label: Demand & Supply
text: Individual vs market

label: Demand & Supply
text: Individual demand: the demand of one buyer.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Market demand: the combined demand of all consumers in the market.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Market Qd at price Pi = Consumer A's Qd at Pi + Consumer B's Qd at Pi + all other buyers' Qd at Pi.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Horizontal summation

label: Demand & Supply
text: At each price, add A's and B's quantities demanded. Repeat for every price.

label: Demand & Supply
text: At P1, B buys nothing, so market Qd = QA1.

label: Demand & Supply
text: At P2, market Qd = QA2 + QB1.

label: Demand & Supply
text: B starts buying below P1, so the market curve has a kink at that price.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Relative Price

label: Demand & Supply
text: Definitions

label: Demand & Supply
text: Normal price: the price of a good expressed in terms of money.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Relative price: the price of a good expressed in terms of another good.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Relative price of X in terms of Y = normal price of X / normal price of Y.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Relative price tells us how much of Y we give up to get one unit of X.

label: Demand & Supply
text: A decrease in the relative price of Good X in terms of Good Y will result in an increase in the proportion of Good X in the total quantity of X and Y consumed, and vice versa, other things being constant.

label: Demand & Supply
text: If one unit of X costs fewer units of Y, people choose a larger proportion of X, other things being constant.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Proportion means the amount of X as a share of the total amount of X and Y. It does not tell us that the number of units of X must rise.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Example 1 — shipping adds the same $100 to each bottle

label: Demand & Supply
text: Bordeaux prices are $500 for fine wine and $100 for table wine. Shipping either bottle to Hong Kong costs $100. Preferences for wine and table wine are assumed to be the same in both regions.

label: Demand & Supply
text: In Bordeaux, one bottle of fine wine costs five bottles of table wine. In Hong Kong, it costs three.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Fine wine: $500 to $600. The price rises by 100/500 × 100% = 20%.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Table wine: $100 to $200. The price rises by 100/100 × 100% = 100%.

label: Demand & Supply
text: The price of fine wine rises by a smaller percentage. Its relative price in terms of table wine therefore falls. Other things being constant, fine wine makes up a larger proportion of consumption. The average quality is higher.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Example 2 — taxi trips after a rise in flagfall

label: Demand & Supply
text: The flagfall is the starting fare. Suppose it rises from $27 to $29 (ΔPlong = ΔPshort = +$2). Both a long trip and a short trip cost $2 more; other fare charges stay the same.

label: Demand & Supply
text: A long trip costs more to begin with, so the $2 increase is a smaller percentage of its fare.

label: Demand & Supply
text: The relative price of a long trip in terms of a short trip falls.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Other things being constant, long trips make up a larger proportion of all taxi trips. The average distance per trip rises.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Example 3 — visits after a cut in the entrance fee

label: Demand & Supply
text: Cost = entrance fee + time/transport cost. Time cost/hr = $100.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Compare a long visit (6 hrs = $700 + 6 × $100 = $1,300) and a short visit (2 hrs = $700 + $100 × 2 = $900) to the same tourist spot. ($1,300 / $900 = 1.4×) Both include the same entrance fee. A long visit also takes more time, so it has a higher total cost when time cost is included.

label: Demand & Supply
text: A cut in the entrance fee reduces both total costs by the same amount. (Long visit: 6 hrs = $300 + 6 × $100 = $900. Short visit: $300 + $100 × 2 = $500. $900 / $500 = 1.8×) This is a smaller percentage fall for the long visit.

label: Demand & Supply
text: The relative cost of a long visit in terms of a short visit rises.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Other things being constant, long visits make up a smaller proportion of all visits. The average length of a visit falls.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Supply

label: Demand & Supply
text: Supply is the set of quantities of a good that producers are willing and able to sell at all corresponding prices over a period of time, other things being constant.

label: Demand & Supply
text: At one price, the amount sellers are willing and able to sell is called quantity supplied (Qs).

label: Demand & Supply
text: Supply schedule example

label: Demand & Supply
text: Individual vs market supply

label: Demand & Supply
text: Individual supply: the supply of one seller.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Market supply: the combined supply of all sellers in the market.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Qs(Pi) = Qs,A(Pi) + Qs,B(Pi) + … + Qs,n(Pi).

label: Demand & Supply
text: Pi means the price we are looking at; A, B, ..., n are the sellers. At this same price, add the quantities they are willing and able to sell. Repeat for each price. This is horizontal summation.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Law of supply

label: Demand & Supply
text: An increase in the price of a good will result in an increase in its quantity supplied, and vice versa, other things being constant.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Higher price → more revenue for each unit sold → sellers are more willing to sell → higher quantity supplied.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Three points to remember about supply

label: Demand & Supply
text: Willing and able: a shop may be willing to sell face masks. If it has run out, it cannot sell any at that time.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Whole curve vs one point: supply is the whole plan at all prices; Qs is the planned quantity at one price.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Same time period and conditions: use the same time period. Along one supply curve, other things affecting supply stay the same. A change in the good's own price changes quantity supplied along the curve; a change in another factor affecting supply shifts the curve.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Market Equilibrium

label: Demand & Supply
text: Excess demand and excess supply

label: Demand & Supply
text: Quantity demanded (Qd): what buyers are willing and able to buy at this price.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Quantity supplied (Qs): what sellers are willing and able to sell at this price.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Quantity transacted (Qt): the quantity actually bought and sold.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Qt = min{Qd, Qs}.

label: Demand & Supply
text: If Qs > Qd, sellers offer fewer units than buyers plan to buy… here sellers offer more than buyers plan to buy, so Qt = Qd. If Qd > Qs, buyers plan more than sellers offer, so Qt = Qs.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Market equilibrium

label: Demand & Supply
text: A state in which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied and there is no tendency for the price to change.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Equilibrium price (Pe): the market-clearing price where Qd = Qs.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Equilibrium quantity (Qe): the quantity demanded and supplied at Pe.

label: Demand & Supply
text: At equilibrium, planned quantities equal actual sales:

label: Demand & Supply
text: Qd = Qs = Qe = Qtransacted.

label: Demand & Supply
text: Buyers can buy the quantity they planned; sellers can sell the quantity they planned.

text: Answer frames and common traps.

label: Exam Skills
text: Answer Frames

label: Exam Skills
text: Definition question

label: Exam Skills
text: Write the definition verbatim:

label: Exam Skills
text: "The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the highest-valued option forgone."

label: Exam Skills
text: Identify-and-explain question

label: Exam Skills
text: State the choice and the highest-valued available option forgone.

label: Exam Skills
text: State the value of that option as the cost.

label: Exam Skills
text: Include the best alternative use of each required resource; exclude only past costs irrecoverable now.

label: Exam Skills
text: Cost-change frame

label: Exam Skills
text: Before the change, the cost is the value of ______.

label: Exam Skills
text: The change affects / does not affect the resources required, the value of this option, or which option is highest-valued.

label: Exam Skills
text: Therefore, cost increases / decreases / remains unchanged / may or may not change.

label: Exam Skills
text: Economic good or free good

label: Exam Skills
text: "It is a good."

label: Exam Skills
text: Compare quantity available with all wants.

label: Exam Skills
text: Add relevant supporting features — never infer "free good" from a zero money price.

label: Exam Skills
text: Three Checks Before You Write

label: Exam Skills
text: Whenever an economic variable changes, ask

label: Exam Skills
text: Which option becomes more or less attractive?

label: Exam Skills
text: Which scarce resource is affected?

label: Exam Skills
text: What is now the highest-valued alternative forgone?

label: Exam Skills
text: Before identifying who should produce what

label: Exam Skills
text: Compare opportunity costs, not absolute productivity.

label: Exam Skills
text: Lower opportunity cost = comparative advantage.

label: Exam Skills
text: Before classifying a statement

label: Exam Skills
text: Is it about the objective world? → positive.

label: Exam Skills
text: Does it involve value judgement? → normative.

label: Exam Skills
text: Is it true by definition or logic? → neither.

label: Exam Skills
text: Common Traps

label: Exam Skills
text: Cost traps

label: Exam Skills
text: Benefit trap: a rise in the value of the chosen option does not by itself change its opportunity cost.

label: Exam Skills
text: Ranking trap: a changed preference order or a new option matters only if it changes the highest-valued option forgone.

label: Exam Skills
text: Past-payment trap: only options available at the decision moment can be forgone.

label: Exam Skills
text: Goods traps

label: Exam Skills
text: Free-of-charge ≠ free good. A free good is defined by whether its quantity is sufficient for all wants, not by its money price.

label: Exam Skills
text: Price is not interest. When you choose Option 2 (buy later), the value is delaying the use of money; the benefit is investment income during the time gained.

label: Exam Skills
text: Demand traps

label: Exam Skills
text: Want ≠ demand. Demand requires willingness and ability to pay.

label: Exam Skills
text: Movement ≠ shift. Own price moves you along the curve; other factors shift it.

label: Exam Skills
text: Proportion ≠ units. A fall in the relative price of X raises X's share, not necessarily its unit count.

label: Exam Skills
text: Allocation traps

label: Exam Skills
text: Money is not required for price competition. Exchanging a collectible toy for a ticket still reflects willingness and ability to pay.

label: Exam Skills
text: Paying money does not automatically make a rule price competition. Check what criterion actually selects the winner.

label: Exam Skills
text: One government service does not a planned economy make. Systems are distinguished by who owns most resources and how they are mainly allocated.

label: Glossary
text: Glossary of Key Terms

label: Glossary
text: Every definition from the notes, in one place.

label: Glossary
text: Scarcity

label: Glossary
text: The situation in which the resources available are not enough to satisfy all people's wants.

label: Glossary
text: Opportunity cost

label: Glossary
text: The value of the highest-valued option forgone at the decision moment.

label: Glossary
text: Full cost

label: Glossary
text: The value of the best alternative uses of all resources (money, time, satisfaction, etc.) necessarily forgone in making a choice. Full cost = explicit cost + implicit cost.

label: Glossary
text: Explicit cost

label: Glossary
text: Money expenditure made as a result of the current choice (e.g. ticket payment).

label: Glossary
text: Implicit cost

label: Glossary
text: The value of the best alternative use of self-owned resources or receipts forgone (earnings, rent, resale value, time).

label: Glossary
text: Positive time preference

label: Glossary
text: People generally prefer the same amount of the same good earlier rather than later, because the value of current consumption exceeds the value of future consumption of the same amount.

label: Glossary
text: Price competition

label: Glossary
text: A type of competition based on users' willingness or ability to pay. The price need not be money.

label: Glossary
text: Non-price competition

label: Glossary
text: A type of competition based on criterion other than willingness or ability to pay — for example age, identity, queueing time, academic results, or a dress code.

label: Glossary
text: Economic good

label: Glossary
text: A good whose quantity is insufficient for all wants. Requires production cost, more is preferred, a price is willing to be paid, and competition arises.

label: Glossary
text: Free good

label: Glossary
text: A good whose quantity is sufficient for all wants. Free-of-charge is not the same as free good.

label: Glossary
text: Private property rights

label: Glossary
text: Exclusive right to use, exclusive right to receive income, and the right to transfer. Clear delineation means it is clear who has each right and what that right allows.

label: Glossary
text: Demand

label: Glossary
text: The set of quantities of a good that consumers are willing and able to buy at all corresponding prices over a period of time, other things being constant.

label: Glossary
text: Quantity demanded (Qd)

label: Glossary
text: The quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at one particular price.

label: Glossary
text: Law of demand

label: Glossary
text: An increase in the price of a good will result in a decrease in its quantity demanded, and vice versa, other things being constant.

label: Glossary
text: Market demand

label: Glossary
text: The combined demand of all consumers in the market, found by horizontal summation.

label: Glossary
text: Relative price

label: Glossary
text: The price of a good expressed in terms of another good. Relative price of X in terms of Y = normal price of X / normal price of Y.

label: Glossary
text: Supply

label: Glossary
text: The set of quantities of a good that producers are willing and able to sell at all corresponding prices over a period of time, other things being constant.

label: Glossary
text: Quantity supplied (Qs)

label: Glossary
text: The quantity sellers are willing and able to sell at one particular price.

label: Glossary
text: Law of supply

label: Glossary
text: An increase in the price of a good will result in an increase in its quantity supplied, and vice versa, other things being constant.

label: Glossary
text: Market equilibrium

label: Glossary
text: A state in which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied and there is no tendency for the price to change. Qd = Qs = Qe = Qtransacted.

label: Glossary
text: Comparative advantage

label: Glossary
text: Producing a good at a lower opportunity cost than another person. Guides who should specialize in what.

label: Glossary
text: Positive statement

label: Glossary
text: A claim about the objective world that is refutable by facts. May be true or false.

label: Glossary
text: Normative statement

label: Glossary
text: A claim involving value judgement (subjective).
